curriculum.lesson_evidence: Punctuating for effect means choosing commas, dashes, colons and sentence boundaries to control pace and emphasis—not sprinkling marks randomly. A dash can interrupt; a colon can announce; a full stop can land a blow.
curriculum.scope_limit: Proposed Stage 4 NESA English alignment using catalogue outcome codes (EN4-*); content-point mapping and independent NESA verification remain pending.

lesson.child_mission: Punctuating for effect means choosing commas, dashes, colons and sentence boundaries to control pace and emphasis—not sprinkling marks randomly. A dash can interrupt; a colon can announce; a full stop can land a blow.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same strategy to an unfamiliar topic or audience, then compare the effect of two different choices.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Revise one overloaded sentence three ways (comma splice fixed; dash interrupt; colon announce) and say which best fits a tense moment.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: all three are grammatical; rationale links mark to effect.

CHECK
Using ellipsis or multiple exclamation marks instead of structured punctuation to fake intensity.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
Independently edit a peer or self paragraph for punctuation effect: make six deliberate changes, label each job, and keep meaning intact.

Write a short reflection describing one specific revision you made and why.
lesson.learning_intention: Punctuating for effect means choosing commas, dashes, colons and sentence boundaries to control pace and emphasis—not sprinkling marks randomly. A dash can interrupt; a colon can announce; a full stop can land a blow.
lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

WORKED MODEL
Compare: 'She pushed and waited and pushed.' vs 'She pushed. She waited. She pushed again—then heard the side latch give.' Shorter sentences and the dash heighten urgency.

TRY FIRST
Revise one overloaded sentence three ways (comma splice fixed; dash interrupt; colon announce) and say which best fits a tense moment.

FEEDBACK
Strong answer: all three are grammatical; rationale links mark to effect.
teach_steps.explain:
Punctuating for effect means choosing commas, dashes, colons and sentence boundaries to control pace and emphasis—not sprinkling marks randomly. A dash can interrupt; a colon can announce; a full stop can land a blow.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner make decisions based on specific language evidence, rather than guess or copy someone else. Keep the meaning accurate and explain the choice.

HOW TO WORK
Read the original example and locate the words or actions that support the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Check your response against the feedback: did you address the same skill and show your reasoning? If a detail is uncertain, identify what would have to be checked. One deliberate, justified revision is more useful than making the answer longer.
